summary.text: Ancient history is the time period from the beginning of writing and recorded human history through late antiquity.
It covers all continents inhabited by humans from 3000 BC to AD 500, and the three-age system divides it into the Stone Age, the Bronze Age, and the Iron Age.
Over this time the world population kept climbing, from an estimated 45 million by 3000 BC to 209 million by AD 500.

paragraphs.heading: What the period covers
paragraphs.text: Ancient history is the part of the human past that starts when people began to write and runs on through late antiquity. Counted this way, recorded history is roughly 5,000 years long, and it opens with Sumerian cuneiform script. The period takes in every continent where people lived between 3000 BC and AD 500.

paragraphs.heading: Stone, bronze and iron
paragraphs.text: One common way to divide this time is the three-age system, which splits it into a Stone Age, then a Bronze Age, then an Iron Age. Recorded history is usually said to begin with the Bronze Age. The ages did not start and stop at the same moment everywhere. In many regions the Bronze Age begins a few centuries before 3000 BC, while the Iron Age ends anywhere from early in the first millennium BC to late in the first millennium AD.

paragraphs.heading: A fast-growing world
paragraphs.text: Across these centuries the number of people grew exponentially, while a change known as the Neolithic Revolution was in full swing. Around 10,000 BC there were perhaps 2 million people, and by 3000 BC there were about 45 million. The count reached 72 million by 1000 BC, in the Iron Age, and roughly 209 million by AD 500. Over 10,500 years, the population multiplied a hundred times.

paragraphs.heading: Before anyone wrote
paragraphs.text: Prehistory is the time before written records. Most of what we know about it comes from the work of archaeologists. Homo erectus spread across Eurasia about 1.8 million years ago. Modern humans, Homo sapiens, appeared somewhere between 250,000 and 160,000 years ago, and some 50,000 years ago they moved out of Africa. They reached Australia around 45,000 years ago and the Americas around 15,000 years ago.

paragraphs.heading: Farms and tame animals
paragraphs.text: Signs of farming show up around 9000 BC in what is now eastern Turkey, and farming then spread through the Fertile Crescent. Sheep and goats were tamed in that same region at about the same time. In China, people were growing millet, rice and legumes by around 7000 BC. Dogs came first among domestic animals, at least 15,000 years ago, and cattle, horses, donkeys and camels followed later. These animals gave food, but they also carried loads and pulled people, which hugely raised how much work humans could get done.

paragraphs.heading: Metal, pots and wheels
paragraphs.text: People hammered copper into objects before they learned to smelt it from ore, which happened around 6000 BC in western Asia. Alloy metalwork started with bronze, in Mesopotamia in about 3500 BC, and China worked it out on its own by 2000 BC. The potter's wheel appeared sometime between 5000 and 4000 BC. By 3000 BC the same idea had become wheeled vehicles, which could haul goods farther and more easily than people or animals alone.

paragraphs.heading: The cradle of civilisation
paragraphs.text: The ancient Near East is often called the cradle of civilisation. It was the first place to farm intensively all year round, and it created one of the earliest coherent writing systems, the potter's wheel and then the wheel for vehicles. It also produced the first central governments, law codes and empires. Alongside them came social ranks, slavery and organised war.
